work.title: History of Karka d-Beth Slok
work.edition: Machine translation (claude-opus-5-5, Patristica, 2026-11-09) of: Paul Bedjan Acta martyrum et sanctorum 2; TEI by J. E. Walters, Digital Syriac Corpus (syriaccorpus.org 486)

paragraphs.text: The History of Karka of Beth Slokh (Kirkuk?) and of the Martyrs in It.

The foundations of this great city were laid by the king of Assyria who in [?] was called Sardana. This king was great and feared throughout the whole world, and his kingdom was one of the three kingdoms of the inhabited earth. This Sardana was the son of Sennacherib, who was the thirty-second king after Belus, the first king of the Assyrians. In the days of this Sardana, Jonah was sent by God to Nineveh, and by his prophecy and preaching he shook the Ninevites. This Sardana submitted to the prophet's preaching, decreed a fast in Nineveh, and the people put on sackcloth. And God saw their repentance, as it is written, and turned the heat of his anger away from them, and did not destroy them. In the fifteenth year of that son of Nimrod, Arbaq, king of Media, [rose up?] against the kingdom of the Assyrians [?]. Through it may the feeble reader, the writer and the congregation that heard the story of the blessed one be gladdened [?], and be made worthy of mercy and compassion on the day of judgment and testing, by the grace of Christ, to whom be glory and thanksgiving, and to his Father and to the Holy Spirit praise, honour, exaltation and dominion, now and always and for ever and ever, yes and amen. Here ends the story of the martyrdom of the blessed Mar Qardagh. To God be glory, amen.

…was, and he showed rebellion. When this Arbaq rebelled against the kingdom of the Assyrians, he gained strength little by little, growing stronger and more powerful until he was a match for the king of Assyria. Once he was strong, he began to make raids on the kingdoms that were subject to the king of Assyria and took territories from them. After that he came raiding into the land of Beth Garmai. At that time its petty king was Garmai, who held the land, and Arbaq carried off captives from him and plundered his domain. The kingdom of this Garmai, the land over which he reigned, stretched from the river Zab as far as the river Tigris; from the Tigris as far as the mountain called Awrok; from that mountain as far as the river Atherqon, which is also called Turmara, and as far as the region of Lereb [?] and the mountain of Sha'ran, and as far as the Lesser Zab itself. Garmai's residence was at Birath Garmai, on that mountain of Awrok, whose buildings are known even now. When this Garmai was hard pressed by the kingdom of Arbaq and could not pay tribute to the kingdom of the Assyrians, he received from the kingdom of the Assyrians a governor over his kingdom, commanders over his domain, and the reinforcement of a troop of soldiers for his band. Then Sargon ordered that in that land

under the dominion of the kingdom of Garmai a city should be built in his name to serve as its capital. In the land of that dominion, to which the whole land was subject as to a harbour [?], it was built in the king's presence to be the head of the dominion of that kingdom. Sargon built it, named the city he built after himself, and made it free. He gave it the whole land in which it was planted to be its servants. He built a royal palace in the city he had planted, and brought and settled in it a great family from the land of the Assyrians, from the nobles of the kingdom: a nobleman whose name was Burzin. He built a small fortress for the city, set it in the plain, and made a small wall for it. With that family and great clan he gathered and settled there about a thousand people from Assyria, some inside the wall and some outside it. In the middle of the city he built Sargon's royal palace and the residence of the governor whom he had installed there. But when the kingdom of Assyria began to fail and Assyrian rule was being destroyed by divine judgment, Arbaq built a wall of strength [?] — he is Adwerbad, over the kingdom of the Medes, after whom the land of Adurbaigan was named — and began to come against Nimrod with a great army. He met [?] that tribe of the Assyrian while it was encamped in Cilicia. They fought a battle, and the Assyrian was overpowered

and was killed in Cilicia. After that the kingdom of the Assyrians came to an end, and the kingdom of the Babylonians reigned. When that too was dissolved, the kingdom of the Medes arose. It too came to an end, and over Persia reigned Darius son of Hystaspes, whom the Magi call the son of Minozihr [?], one of the kings who reigned in Persia. He fought a battle with Alexander son of Philip and was defeated by him, and Alexander took away the kingdom of Darius. Alexander reigned over the kingdom of the Greeks, and since he had no sons, he divided his kingdom among four of his servants, who took over his kingdom after his death. One of them was named Seleucus. He built five cities: Antioch, the city of Syria; Seleucia of Syria; Seleucia of Pisidia; Seleucia, the great city of Beth Aramaye; and the city of Karka of Beth Slokh. After Sardana, this city was settled by Darius, who built a wall for it outside the wall that the king of Assyria had built. He built houses in it, and a fire temple next to the temple of idols that Sardana had set up there; and the eagle and the earth were worshipped there. Darius brought five families from the land of Istakhr and settled them in the city; their names are written in the archives of the kingdom of Persia. After Darius came Seleucus, king of the Greeks, who was mentioned above.

He turned the city wall that his servant had built into a mound, and on top of it built a high wall. For the wall he built he made towers—that is, bastions—sixty-five of them. He made one gate on the south-east side and another gate on the north-west. Over the south-eastern gate he set, at its full height, a carving of stone, and to the right and left of this gate, towers of stone and lime. This gate was the king's. The other was called after the man under whose direction it was built: Totai. Within the city Seleucus built a royal palace, and he adorned and laid out the city with streets and squares, and greatly enlarged it, not only inside the wall but outside it as well. He divided it into seventy-two streets, and brought five noble families from Istakhr and settled them in it, together with the rest of the people whom he brought from various places. To these five families he brought he gave lands and vineyards in the district, and he left the city free of tribute. Twelve streets were named after twelve noble families, and the rest were named after the crafts. And in memory of King Sardana, who first built the city, Seleucus built a hall of [?] beside the royal palace that he had built within the fortress; to this day it is called Sarboi.

So the city remained in paganism from the time it was built until the coming of the holy apostles Addai and Mari, who were sent by the Holy Spirit to preach in our land. When they entered the city, they were welcomed by a man named Joseph. When he had become a disciple and been baptized by them, he built the church that is today called the monastery of Beth Joseph. From then on the seed of faith in Christ grew in the city; many received baptism and became true Christians. From the time of King Valash until the years of Shapur son of Ardashir, a span of ninety years, the blessed city was a field with no tares in it. But in the time of Shapur, Mani, who was wholly evil, belched out [?] his satanic gall, and it sprouted two tares, named Addai and Abzakhya, sons of the evil one. In the time of Ardawan, king of the Arsacids, and in the reign of Hadrian Caesar, when persecution grew fierce against the churches in the regions of the west, shepherds and leaders from there came fleeing to the land of the east. To the city there came, as head and leader, a godly man named Theocritus. With the permission of the head who was in Shahrgard, this Theocritus became bishop in Karka and was reckoned second to him. For the metropolitan rank had been given by the apostles and by the throne

of Antioch to Shahrgard; second was Theocritus, third the see of Lashom, fourth that of Herbath Glal, and fifth that of Dara. This Theocritus built a church for the people of Karka, and ordered and established in it the apostolic canons and rules by which the ministry of the clergy of Karka is conducted to this day. The church that Theocritus built is the one that John, the excellent shepherd and splendid priest, later renewed. After the departure of Theocritus, Abdisho received his throne, and bishops arose one after another until the time of Maana, bishop and victorious martyr. In his days there was a persecution of the Christians, and the church was torn down, for rebellion appeared even among the people of Karka themselves, and it was some of them who tore down the church of their own city. The persecution in Karka came not only through killing but also through plundering of property, chains and bitter scourgings. Even women, Daughters of the Covenant consecrated to virginity, who had come from the royal city because of the persecution of the church there and were living in our city, were denounced before Peygan the Salar by Manichaean people who were in the city. And that accursed man ordered them to be killed outside the city, at a place called Hawra.

After the holy women had been crowned, in the place where they were crowned a palm tree sprang up from their blood, and it brought healing to those who took refuge in it. But when the Manichaeans saw the wonder that had taken place, they cut down the palm and burned its place with fire. Yet God, who does not let his mercies be scorned by enemies, set upon them the disease of leprosy, which disfigured them, until they came to an end and vanished from the city. The place where the holy women were victorious is called Beth Tetha, "the House of the Palm," to this day, and it has now been made a place of refuge for all believers. Every year, when the commemoration of the great day of the Crucifixion is completed and the people go up to the great martyrion, as is the city's custom, the whole assembly of the church—the shepherd and his flock in all its ranks, with the cross at their head and going before them—turns aside to Beth Tetha in great pomp, with praises and holy songs of thanksgiving befitting God the Lord of all, to the shame of unbelievers and the glory of believers. And upon us sinners be mercy, compassion and salvation, amen. So much for this. Because of the severity of the persecution, a few people from Karka, with their shepherd, a mighty hero, made small buildings like a church in a cave beside the city, in the rough ground of an estate called Hasa, and there they secretly received the holy mysteries. When the erring pagans discovered the valiant athlete,

they went there after him and fell upon him like ravenous, merciless beasts. When they saw that he would not consent to their will or exchange truth for falsehood, they stoned him on the slope above Hasa, and he received the crown of martyrdom by stoning. After him the blessed Isaac, of a noble family, rose to the leadership, and he too was crowned with martyrdom. He was stoned by freemen of Karka who called themselves by the name of Christians, but were compelled by the king's command. He was stoned on the mound above the edge of the village of Beniqatur Awna [?]. After him arose John, who shone, together with Mar Jacob bishop of Nisibis and John bishop of Arbela, at the holy council of the three hundred and eighteen. After John arose Aqebalaha. When this blessed man was about fifteen years old, he began works of virtue and gave alms, so much so that he would secretly take gold, silver and clothing from his parents and distribute them to strangers. His father, who was at the king's court and held the rank of administrator of Bazdai [?], heard of it, and to please the king he denied Christ and worshipped fire. But the blessed man left his father's house and went out into exile.

Because of his great labours and glorious victories, he was chosen to take charge of the church of his city. When he took office, he rebuilt the church that had been torn down in the days of Maana. He gave it vessels of gold and silver, with silks, utensils and [?], to complete its service. After his parents died, he gave the church the whole treasure he found belonging to them. He made many disciples and baptized them. Among these was also the village called Tishin, which got that name from the ninety families that King Shapur brought from Maishan and planted there. They worshipped the demon Nani, whom they had brought with them from their own land. One of the five parts of the village was the inheritance of the blessed man's parents; formerly it was called Kewsarwan [?], after the name of the blessed man's parents. This village the victorious man made into disciples and brought into the fold of life. And because of the signs and wonders that the heavenly power worked through his hands, the report of his victories spread and reached Bahram son of Shapur, king of Persia, who had a daughter tormented by an unclean demon. When the holy Aqebalaha was summoned there, he laid his hand on the girl and she was healed. And he persuaded the king that the churches should not be torn down, and that those which had been torn down

should be rebuilt. The king listened to him, and it was done as he wished. The two tares that appeared in the victorious man's time, Mani and Zaradusht, he uprooted and abolished. There was also the unbelief and rebellion that appeared in two of the families that Sardana had brought and planted in Karka, whose names are these: Parin, the one who denied, and Balash, the one who rebelled. To Parin son of Amalka and to Balash fell this evil inheritance in Karka. This evil seed the victorious Aqebalaha uprooted, and he refuted them in his disputations. Nevertheless they persisted, sometimes openly and sometimes secretly, in the bitter root of the accursed Mani until the time of Khusro, and then they too came to an end. After Aqebalaha, God's devout one, fell asleep, the flock of the people of Karka chose Barhadbeshabba, for he was attested by signs and wonders and by every excellent work. When this blessed man too fell asleep, a stranger [?] arose after him, a man perfect, humble and complete in righteousness. When this victorious man too departed to his Lord, his throne was received by the chosen and excellent Mar Shapur son of Raz, of the city, adorned with spiritual beauties. His family is the one called Beth Ardashir son of Shapur Raz. But this chosen man left the leadership and went out to the monastery of the mourners, and there he served with them splendidly, in all purity

and holiness. With the sword of the Spirit that he held, he uprooted the tares of Mani and cleansed the field of Karka of them. The members of his own family, who were from the family that Seleucus had brought from the land of Istakhr, he made into pure vessels for the name of the Creator. From their inheritance he built a house for strangers, in which the sick, the weary, the poor and the needy are received and refreshed. He gave the house, and set apart for it, property to pay the physicians who are there and to provide whatever is needed by those who come to be healed. When he was gathered in peace to his Lord, there arose after him the victorious athlete, the chaste priest and temple of holiness, Mar John, who was perfected in both, namely in priesthood and in martyrdom. In his time Yazdgard, who was the fifth after Shapur, was reigning in the land of Persia. Like Shapur, he too stirred up persecution against the church of God, although until his seventh year he had conducted himself mildly. In his eighth year he killed his daughter, who was also his wife, and the nobles of his kingdom. He went to the land of Tashol and subdued the petty kings there, and he built a city there and called it after himself, Shahristan Yazdgard. While he was there he drove the Christians out of his camp, for the wretch thought that it was because of the Christians that his enemies were defeating him. He picked out eight thousand Magian men and deprived them

of their manhood, and appointed them to his service; many of them died from this sentence. There was a custom among the kings of Persia that at every new moon, for seven days, each of the nobles would come in and plead the cause of the oppressed, and make known before the king all matters that were being badly handled. This custom that wicked man abolished. When he returned from Tashol and came to his royal residence, he wrote to Tahmyazdgard Munrazdbed [?], who was in Nisibis and was learned in the order of Magianism, that the Sarosh and Razrad [?] of the land of Arzon, named Adurfrazgard, and the Dastbirham-rad [?] of Adiabene and Beth Garmai, named Surin, should go with him. The three of them were to go to Karka, and with persuasion and gifts compel the Christians of the four regions governed by the four rulers mentioned above to deny Christ and worship fire. And if they would not worship the sun, nor sacrifice to fire and water, they were to be handed over to scourging, to the combs, and to death by the sword. Tahmyazdgard and those with him came and entered Karka on the fifteenth of the month of Tammuz. They scourged the leaders, the freemen and the rest of the nobles in Karka and threw them into prison. And they sent merciless troops

to distant regions and commanded them: "Whatever Christians you find, bring them here in heavy chains. If they do not deny their faith, they shall perish by various deaths." When John, bishop of Karka, saw what had happened, he wrote to the patriarch of Antioch asking that prayers be offered for him and his flock, that God would help them and bring them out victorious from this contest to which they had been called. From the day Tahmyazdgard entered Karka, from the fifteenth of Tammuz until the twentieth of the month of Ab, the holy John did not leave the sanctuary. Instead he and his flock stayed gathered in the church, calling on God with groaning to come to their help. In those days Tahmyazdgard gave orders, and they separated the shepherd from his flock and threw him into prison with a multitude of Christians who were imprisoned there, and they kept pressing him to worship the sun. As he came out of his Lord's house to go, and saw the judge, he said to Tahmyazdgard in a loud voice: "Peace to you, judge who will be judged! Peace to you, persecutor who will be won over [?]! Peace to you, Magian who will confess and become a martyr! A great company has been made ready for you, Tahmyazdgard, with which you will raise a shout before the Bridegroom who has invited us to his kingdom. For behold, I see you:

like Simon Peter, you too are destined to be hung on a cross head downward for the name of Christ." Imprisoned with the blessed John were great men from a noble family in Karka: one of them was Isaac son of Hormizdgard, along with Ardashir son of Arzanaya, Abraham, and seven others with them. Some of them stood firm in their truth, and some denied. While Isaac son of Hormizd was in chains for the fear of God, this blessed man opened his mouth and spoke to Tahmyazdgard prophetically, in words like those the blessed John had said to him: "You are destined, O Tahmyazdgard, to be crowned with a good martyrdom for our Lord's sake. Instead of a wolf you will become a lamb, and you will offer your body as a sacrifice, living, holy and acceptable, pleasing to God." Tahmyazdgard immediately gave orders, and the possessions and livestock of the people of Karka were plundered by pagans and Manichaeans. Those who had been ordered to gather and bring Christians from every place went out in savage fury, and they gathered and brought not only lay men and women but also bishops, priests and deacons: namely the metropolitan of Arbela, the bishop of Beth Nuhadra, and the bishop of Maalta; and with them the metropolitan of Shahrgard, and his second, John of Karka.

and the third, of Lashom; the fourth, of Mahoza; the fifth, of Herbath Glal; and the sixth, of Dara, the village on the bank of the Lesser Zab. These pastors, with their clergy and a multitude from their flocks, came gladly to Karka to receive the crowns of martyrdom with great joy. As they entered, the cross of their glory went at their head, and they honored it with careful liturgy and with hallelujahs. According to the account, they numbered a hundred and thirty-three thousand, not counting the people of Karka held in prison, who numbered twenty thousand. When those in prison heard the thunder of the liturgy of those who had come, all of them assemblies made ready for the kingdom, they rejoiced with very great joy. But when Tahmizgard and his men saw how large the assemblies were and heard the loud sound of their praises, they were badly shaken, because they thought it was a revolt. Tahmizgard went up to the place called Beth Teta, where martyrs had been killed in the days of King Shapur. He sat on the judgment seat and set out before those assemblies all kinds of instruments of torture, and said to them: “King Yazdgird has commanded this: if you do not obey his rule and his commands, and do not do his will, and do not worship the sun, the great god, and do not

honor fire and water, the children of Hormizd, you will lose your lives by these.” Along with the instruments there were also sixteen elephants, which they had brought to trample all who would not deny Christ. But the blessed Isaac picked up the instruments of torture, kissed them, laid them on his eyes and said: “Peace to these irons, by which we enter the palace of the kingdom on high and delight in the tents of light that our Lord Christ prepared for us before the foundations of the world.” Then he spoke to the judge: “Why are you standing there, judge? Come now and do what you have been commanded. All of us are ready to die joyfully for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” When the judge heard this, he gave the order, and they stretched the holy Isaac out on the ground by his four limbs and drove stakes through his hands and his feet. They tore at his body with iron combs until the flesh was stripped from his bones. While he lay stretched out on the rock of Beth Teta and the wicked kept tearing at him, so that his blood ran down and flowed to the plain at Beth Teta, and while the saint was being tortured, Tahmizgard gave orders that all who were imprisoned for Christ should be brought to the court beside Beth Teta and questioned. Whoever did not deny the name of Christ was to be tortured like Isaac. But the people

of the holy and chosen Christians knew that the time of their crowning had come. So the pastors gathered in the church with their flocks, celebrated the Eucharist and received the life-giving mysteries. They embraced one another and exchanged the holy kiss. Then they went out carrying the cross and walked in procession all the way to Beth Teta. When they saw the holy Isaac stretched out with his body being torn by combs, they raised their voices and gave glory to God. They strengthened and encouraged the blessed man so that he would not lose heart in these torments. The judge then gave orders, and they brought naphtha, smeared it on the saint’s bones and set them on fire. As the flames crackled in the victor’s bones and he was about to depart to his Lord, he raised his voice and blessed the ranks of the Israel of God, and was crowned with a good martyrdom. After him the judge ordered them to bring the glorious priest John, bishop of Karka. They brought him to the place where they had stretched out the victorious Isaac and cut off his hands, and his blood ran down and flowed to that same plain of Beth Teta. Then they brought him, along with the sixty others who were with him, to the valley east of Beth Teta. The saints ran there eagerly, singing the psalms of David, and came to the place that sloped down into the snare of death. The judge gave orders, and the king’s letter was read out before them.

It offered ranks, gifts and positions of authority to everyone who would deny Christ. For everyone who refused to be persuaded and deny him, it promised the sword, fire, scourging and iron combs. The saints answered with one voice: “Let the king keep his gifts for himself, and let him give positions and ranks to others. We have a treasure in heaven that never passes away, and from there we await our Life-giver, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body so that it will be like his glorious body.” When the judge heard this, he passed sentence on the victorious ones. Some had their feet cut off, some had their tongues cut out, some had their eyes gouged out, and some had the skin of their heads flayed. Then, to bring their contest to its end, the judge gave orders, and they brought reeds and brushwood and looked for pitch to smear on the wood. No pitch could be found in our region, so they smeared it with naphtha. They placed the saints in the middle, with John the bishop at their head, set the wood on fire and burned the bodies of the athletes. In this way they were made perfect in martyrdom for Christ. Their number was as follows: the bishop; Dadishoʿ, Shubhalishoʿ and Bokhtishoʿ, the priests who were with him; and twenty-eight notable believers of Karka. These were crowned on the first day, the twenty-fourth of the month of Ab, a Friday, in the sixth week after the Fast of the Apostles.

On the twenty-fifth of the same month, a Saturday, they brought out three thousand of the inhabitants of Karka, whose names are written in the book of life, to the place where the first company had been crowned. Tahmizgard went out, altars were built, and they tried to force the people of Karka to sacrifice. But they cried out, made strong by their God, and said: “Far be it from us to abandon Christ, who became a sacrifice for us, and sacrifice to rebellious demons.” The more he afflicted them with severe torments, the stronger they grew in Christ. The deacons of the clergy among them, whose names were Isaac [?], were stoned on the slope above the edge [?] of the town. Two women, daughters of the covenant from Karka, were crucified halfway up that slope and stoned on their crosses. For Abraham, Simeon and Maʿne they dug a pit at the top of the slope, where Stephen and his companions had been stoned, and brought them there loaded with heavy irons. The rest of that blessed band of three thousand were crowned at the place where John’s company had been burned on the first day. As for Abraham, Simeon and Maʿne, mentioned above, archers were sent against them and shot them with arrows in the pit where they sat. Then they heated awls and pierced

the pupils of their eyes, and with other awls glowing from the fire they pierced the victors’ bodies. These were crowned on the second day, the twenty-fifth of Ab, a Saturday. On Sunday, the third day of the victors’ crowning, Tahmizgard gave orders, and they brought out to the place of the court eight thousand nine hundred and forty souls. These had been brought from villages and towns far and near, and with them were the metropolitan of Shahargard and the bishops of Lashom, Mahoza, Herbath Glal and the village of Dara. When they had all been gathered, he set the bishops apart by themselves in chains, and brought in the rest of the saints group by group for questioning. All of them confessed Christ and none denied him. When the pagans saw that they were all of one soul and one mind, the judge set about three thousand insolent and pitiless Magians on them. Some of the saints they put to the sword, and others they handed over to the burning fire. Some were sawn apart and some were stoned. Others had vinegar and mustard poured into their mouths, eyes and nostrils until they died. In short, by scourgings and every kind of death

they released the victors from this world, so that they could pass to their own place and go to their inheritance, which is light, life and peace. Then one of the officials with Tahmizgard was sent to the bishops mentioned above. He came and asked them, “Who is your head?” All of them were silent. But a boy was imprisoned there, the son of a widow of Karka, whose name was Dindoy, like the first Dindon in the days of Shapur. It was because of this Dindon that the rank of metropolitan came to Karka. He stood up bravely and said to the fathers: “Take courage in our Lord, our fathers, and do not be afraid. Give the enemies an answer. If you will not, hand over the leadership of Karka to us, and we will receive the tortures of the persecutors in your place.” At that very hour the metropolitan of Shahargard and the bishops with him agreed, and they wrote it down in a document, sealed it and said: “O boy, the rank of metropolitan rightly belongs to you, because you have become a second Elijah and a young David in this hour of trial.” From that day the primacy of the metropolitan see was established in Karka. Still in their chains, they laid their hands on him and blessed him. When the pagans saw that the Christians stood firm in their glory and kept their rules without fear, they put them to the sword. First they killed

the glorious Dindon, and then the bishops and the others with them, some from Karka and some from various other places. Now there was a woman from the neighborhood of Beth Zadoq named Shirin, who baked bread in her house. When she heard that the saints had been crowned, she left her bread and her dough in the kneading trough and took her two sons with her, one on her shoulder and one by the hand. She ran and found the judge Tahmizgard below Hawra. Seizing the bridle of the horse he was riding, she adjured him in Persian not to keep her from the road by which the holy martyrs had been sent on. The judge turned toward her, astonished. He tried to persuade the woman to give up the conviction she held so firmly, and when she would not be persuaded, he passed sentence on her. Her head was cut off with the sword, along with that of her elder son. Her little son threw himself on the bodies of his mother and brother, weeping. He took some of their blood and smeared it on his eyes and his body. However often the judge and the pagans pulled him over to themselves and tried to coax him with gifts and words, he kept running back to the bodies of his mother and brother, throwing himself on them and kissing them as he wept. Then the accursed men killed him too. After these had been killed, the Lord opened the eyes of Tahmizgard, and he saw a ladder set up on the earth, with its top reaching

to heaven. All those he had killed were climbing up it, and the Lord stood above it, placing glorious and splendid crowns on them. At once the judge turned to repentance and cried out in a loud voice, “I am a Christian,” just as the prophecies about him had foretold. He lamented over himself and wept, begging Christ to forgive him the blood of the martyrs that he had shed. When King Yazdgird heard that Tahmizgard had abandoned Magianism and confessed Christ, he ordered him to be interrogated under the lash. They subjected him to torture, chains, imprisonment, beatings and iron combs, and when they saw that he did not falter in the contest, the king ordered him to be hung on a cross head downward. In this way the blessed Tahmizgard was crowned with a good martyrdom on the twenty-fifth of the month of Elul, a Monday. At the time of his crowning he prayed and asked God that anyone who calls on the name of Tahmizgard in any trial or sickness whatever should receive help from God. This, then, is how these twelve thousand martyrs were crowned, and how they were made perfect with the crowns of victory. Through their prayers may our Lord make us all worthy of their true hope and their glorious delight. Afterward the blessed Maron, bishop of Karka, through the mercy of God that was with him, built at the place where

the victors were crowned a monastery, and every year he held a commemoration for them with the warm fervor of his faith. Together with Mar Babai the Catholicos he convened a synod of the bishops of Beth Garmai and also of Adiabene. They wrote, sealed and handed down a firm decree that there should be a feast in memory of these saints for three days each year: the Friday, Saturday and Sunday of the sixth week after the Fast of the Apostles. This was because the metropolitan of Adiabene was also crowned there, as were the bishop of Beth Nuhadra, the bishop of Maalta and the others with them, who were crowned in that great company of victors. It is also written and kept in the archives of the church of the metropolitan city that any bishop of the eparchy of Karka who neglects to come to the gathering of the victorious martyrs, except because of illness or some necessity that arises, but neglects it of his own will and despises the canon laid down by the fathers, has no authority, by the word of our Lord, to carry out his ministry. This is the wonderful victory of the saints and the glorious labor of the contest of the radiant martyrs and valiant athletes. It has been well told in brief, for I think this is enough, even though lovers of learning are eager to hear more. But we, my brothers, heirs and children of the saints and children of the inheritance of Christ who crowned them,

let us take refuge in their prayers and entreat their Lord, the Lord of all, to pour out his peace, his tranquility and his mercies on every end of creation. May he guard his church by his grace, with the glory of the saints within it, until he is revealed from heaven, and may he adorn it with the delight of its splendid and excellent shepherds, as he promised it. On this holy mountain, a second Sinai, the dwelling of the divine presence, the shining tent of light where the bones of the saints are laid, may praise multiply and thanksgiving increase, and may its horn be raised as high as heaven by the power of the victors, the holy stones laid in its courts. May he make the excellent workers within it shine, those who serve the Lord and are pleasing to him. May divine goodness show them to be ministers of righteousness and holiness, as beloved children of the victorious martyrs. As for the man of God, victorious in the service of the Lord, the superior of his holy house, rich in virtues, who serves his fathers’ house zealously [?]: may the Lord give his hands the double portion of the right hand, with every increase of blessing from heaven and from earth, through the prayers of the saints, and may he be made worthy of the light in their tents. May our Lord Jesus Christ, God over all, make our community too, in all its ranks and orders, worthy of that light and that glory. Amen. We also make known that our fathers established long

ago that on Friday there should be the commemoration of the victorious martyrs: the metropolitan, the bishops, the priests, the deacons and the blessed flock of twelve thousand who were crowned for Christ. On Saturday there should be the commemoration of the holy apostles, the fathers of the victorious martyrs. What bitter death did these wicked judges leave untried, instead of bringing it on the martyrs of mighty strength? What harsh tortures and cruel torments did the enemies of the church forgo, instead of making Christ’s true servants endure them? Or what cup of suffering and bitterness did the enemies of our people neglect, instead of making those valiant ones drink it as they struggled with all their strength in their afflictions? Some they tormented with hunger and thirst until their bodies wasted away and they died. Others were hung head downward in the midday heat until their flesh peeled away and they died. In others, the dislocation [?] of their shoulders, as men stretched them, tore them apart, and they died. Others were beaten every day with harsh blows until their sides [?] were covered in wounds, and they died. Others had their backs and bones broken with heavy clubs, and they died. Others were thrown out bound and naked into the cold and frost until their bodies froze stiff, and they died.

Some had their flesh taken from their bones with razors, carefully, a little at a time, and they died. Others had their skin stripped from them in a cruel flaying, and they died. Others had the joints of their backs sawn through in haste, and they died. Others had their legs pierced with drills, violently and with great pain, and they died. Others had reed splinters laid along their bodies, with cords pulled tight over them, and then pulled out one by one with flesh and sinews, and they died. Others were mercilessly crushed with stones, and they died. Besides other tortures, they cut off their noses, cut off their ears and fingers, put out their eyes, and broke their legs and knees with hammers. Some they hung by the soles of their feet. Others had potsherds packed under their armpits [?], and they died. Others they filled sacks [?] with ashes and thrust their heads into them. Others had vinegar and mustard poured into their nostrils and also rubbed into their wounds. Others had needles driven mercilessly under their fingernails. Others, in the streets [?], not allowing their sores to heal [?], had their scourgings renewed day after day. And after all these
pains and these severe and harsh tortures, they cut off their heads with the sword.
Here ends the history of Karka of Beth Slokh, and of the holy martyrs who were crowned in it and were victorious in a noble martyrdom for the sake of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
